title: Discovering Opinion Intervals from Conflicts in Signed Graphs

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Theorem 2.2 explicitly states that the proposed reduction is invalid: “the interval assignments encoding acyclic partitions rely on strict ordering assumptions that do not hold in all interval configurations” and “the NP-hardness claim ... remains open.” Nevertheless, Appendix A.3 presents the same construction as a completed proof and concludes that it “complet[es] the proof of Theorem 2.2.” These cannot both be true. The appendix therefore does not establish NP-hardness, and all stated hardness consequences relying on it are unproved.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2.1, paragraph beginning “The theorem has several implications”; Abstract; Conclusion
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Despite Theorem 2.2 admitting that its reduction fails and that NP-hardness remains open, the paper still claims hardness consequences: inapproximability within any factor, no FPT algorithm parameterized by edge deletions, NP-hardness under a positive-edge-cycle restriction, and “strong hardness results” in the conclusion. None follows from a theorem whose proof is acknowledged to be invalid. The abstract likewise describes “preliminary hardness results,” but the body and conclusion phrase them as established results.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2.1, claim that the hardness result “implies that detecting these forbidden structures is NP-hard for incomplete signed graphs”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: This implication is false as written. Detecting chordless cycles and other standard forbidden induced subgraphs in an ordinary graph is polynomial-time, and under the claimed restriction the positive-edge graph G+ is itself explicitly a chordless cycle, so detecting that structure is trivial. A hardness result for finding a conflict-free signed-interval representation would not imply that detection of chordless cycles is NP-hard.

predicted_errors.error_location: Proof of Theorem 2.3, paragraph enumerating “all possible overlap-patterns of k intervals”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The proof treats every one of the 2^(k choose 2) binary overlap relations as a possible family of intervals. This is wrong: overlap graphs of intervals must be interval graphs, while many graphs on k vertices are not interval graphs. Enumerating all binary patterns is only safe if non-realizable patterns are discarded. As written, the algorithm may select a non-interval overlap pattern with a better objective and return an assignment that cannot be represented by any k intervals, invalidating the claimed BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION guarantee.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2.2 versus Theorem 2.3 and Appendix B
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Theorem 2.3 and Appendix B claim a PTAS for complete graphs with arbitrary fixed k intervals. But the Section 2.2 overview subsequently says that “overlapping intervals introduce intricate dependencies,” that greedy assignments are only approximate, and that “the general case requires further algorithmic innovations beyond current methods.” This directly contradicts the asserted general PTAS theorem rather than merely describing a limitation of an implementation.

The approximate counts displayed in the Figure 8 table sum to about 2,600 politicians: LINKE about 250, GRÜNE about 400, SPD about 750, FDP about 300, CDU/CSU about 700, and AfD about 200. The dataset is stated throughout the paper, including Table 1 and Table 2, to contain only |V| = 1,480 politicians, and each politician is assigned to one interval. The displayed assignment counts therefore cannot describe this dataset.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix C.2, text immediately following Table 3
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text says that “WikiConflict [is] the only dataset with more than 1% improvement” above 8-Chains.
